title: Inspect a schematic before gathering materials
summary: Measure the footprint, inspect hidden collection layers and estimate survival materials from a schematic.

body.text: Before gathering materials, answer three questions about the file: how much space the build occupies, what sits below ground, and what the stored blocks cannot tell you about startup.

head: Extension
How to inspect it
rows: Open the build in a compatible schematic viewer. Orbit the model for an overview, then switch to individual horizontal layers.
Use a viewer that reads Bedrock structures, such as Schemat.io.
Import the file as a playable Bedrock world. B172 uses this format, so you can watch the farm operate inside the download.

body.text: Read the model from the bottom up

items: Find the output chest in the full model and choose a fixed corner as your reference. Measure the width, depth and height. If you measure by coordinates, count both end blocks: from X=10 through X=17 is eight blocks wide.
Hide the layers above the collector. Find the lowest hopper or transport channel and record how far below the planting surface it sits. That gives you the excavation depth before you lay the floor.

Raise the visible layer one block at a time. Trace where each item lands, which hopper receives it, and which container that hopper feeds. Check the same corner each time so a camera rotation does not reverse your layout.

Read the material counts and split them into loads. For example, 145 ordinary stackable building blocks take two full stacks plus 17. Add any access path or extra storage you plan to build outside the file.

body.text: A visible hopper tells you where a hopper goes. It does not establish which items belong in a filter, how much fuel to supply, or whether a clock starts enabled. Check the creator’s operating sequence for those details. In a test copy, feed one item into the intake and watch it reach the intended chest before copying the section.

body.label: Load the schematic in Minecraft Java

body.text: Viewer references: Schemalook’s ruler, layer mode and block list, and Schemat.io’s supported 3D preview formats.
